groups.text: G one, the default collector, keeps eden, survivor and old, but not as three big spaces.
It cuts the heap into equal regions.
A region is the max heap divided by two thousand forty-eight, kept between one and thirty-two MB, and rounded up to a power of two.
A one GB heap gets one MB regions.
Each region has a role for a while: eden, survivor, old, humongous, or free.
New objects fill the eden regions.
A young pause copies the live objects out of every eden and survivor region, into free regions that become survivors.
The evacuated regions are free again, and next time any of them can become anything.
An object larger than half a region is humongous.
It skips eden and gets its own run of whole regions, side by side, which count as old from the start.
A three MiB array plus its sixteen-byte header needs four one MB regions, and nearly all of the fourth is wasted.
Old regions fill up slowly with promoted objects.
When they pass a threshold, forty-five percent of the heap to begin with, G one marks the live objects in the background, while your code keeps running.
Now it knows how much of each old region is still live.
Then come mixed pauses.
They take all the young regions, plus a few old ones: the ones with the most garbage.
That choice is where the name Garbage First comes from.
Copying costs what is live, so a mostly garbage region gives back the most space for the least work.
A region more than eighty-five percent live is not even a candidate.
So, a check.
Which old region does G one take first: one that is seventy percent live, or one that is twenty percent live?
The twenty percent one.
G one copies a fifth of a region, and gets the whole region back.
